title: Calm and Permission
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching is that our perception of reality is often limited by our habitual patterns of attention and blind spots, which can lead to missed opportunities for understanding and connection. By becoming aware of these limitations and cultivating mindfulness, we can develop a more open and non-judgmental awareness, allowing us to find ease and liberation from suffering. This involves embracing both the aspects of our nature that may seem contradictory, such as karmic beings and bodhisattvas, rather than trying to reject or accept one over the other.

Really liking that soup today.

Activated and reactivated and activating each other constantly.

Where does my karmic being stop and yours begin?
It's hard to know.

Crammed in together, doing the same schedule.

Like, why was he, what was he talking about exactly?

So, not to spend too long, and it's a little bit disturbing, but just because it's very karmic: the discussion is mostly [unclear: "consolated"] around three Zen teachers practicing and teaching in America.
Two born in Japan.
One a Native American, not Native American, but you know what I mean, an American-born person.
Initiating sexual contact with students, even in the interview room.
Even during this kind of exact event that we're going through.

I was thinking about it, and it might be that those sanghas either passively or actively allowed that to happen out of some confusion between these two: the karmic being and the vow being, the bodhisattva being.

It might be, when Buddhism was first established, and I came along a little later so I'm speculating, but it might be that when Buddhism first really took root in convert American sanghas like this one, there was a strong belief that we could get rid of the karmic being and only have the vow being.
Only the beautiful, enlightened, awakened, whatever you call it.
And maybe they thought that these teachers had done that.
And that this was so precious, such a wonder, a treasure of the world, that it was worth putting up with or looking the other way.
I don't know.
Maybe they just couldn't see the karmic nature of their teachers.
And there's been a lot of discussion about the possible psychology of these teachers.
Maybe because they became monks as boys and never understood about sexuality or women or something like this.
Who knows, really.
I just wanted to add a little bit there.
Sorry to bring that disturbing image to mind.
It's just to give a little context of where that response that Norman put on the Sweeping Zen website came from.
And if you want to learn more about this, there's sadly vast amounts of information on that same website, going back many years too, which makes it all the more sad.
So our practice isn't a process of trying to shuck off our karmic being.
We know that when we relate to our karmic being in a certain way, we suffer a lot.
We can find that out very experientially and very directly.
We can experience that when we embrace the possibility, just the possibility, of our life beyond the karmic being.
There can at times be some ease, or maybe a change in relationship to our karma.
And it might be that our task is not to reject our karmic being and also not to accept our karmic being.
Not to buy into its persuasive whispering in our ear that this is all there is.
You will never change.
You are stuck.
And not to try to whisper to our other ear, I can't get out of it.
We can't get out of it and we're not stuck in it.
You might have noticed on the altar we have up our Parinibbana Buddha.

Concrete Buddha, you know.
But then somebody, I don't know who did this, made this beautiful pine arrangement that just fits so perfectly with the Parinibbana Buddha.
And in the meantime people started dying.
So we have on this side altar, with Manjushri, the Bodhisattva of wisdom, names of people who have died recently who are close to sangha members.
And I know there are many more people than that.
And there are names on the list for tonight's ceremony.
So it seemed like the Parinibbana Buddha should look after our departed loved ones for a little while longer.
So we left him up on the altar.
And one of the names on the altar is the Shambhala adept, Paul Warwick, who died recently, a couple of weeks ago.
Paul and his wife Jenny were in the original batch of students who gathered around Trungpa Rinpoche in Colorado in the late 1960s, I think, or early 70s.
Not sure when exactly.
And Paul was really kind to me, and I didn't ever work with him formally.
Not until his body was there did I go to Shambhala Center.
So maybe he had me [unclear: "in the inn"], brought me to Shambhala Center by dying.
But he used to have coffee with me.
And he was willing to have coffee with me more than I did, but I was too busy, too caught in my own karma, I guess.
His wife Jenny received titles and has become, is still, an important Shambhala Center teacher.
But Paul never took any titles, never had any special words to his name that I know about anyway.
If he did, he didn't tell me.
Maybe he has a Tibetan name, I don't know.
He used to tell me teachings in a very plain-spoken way.

He would just talk about his own practice.
And one of the last times I saw him, he said, "Well, my practice now is to neither accept nor reject anything."
That really struck me, like, huh.
I understand the suffering of rejection.
To not accept is interesting.
What does that mean?
Maybe he was talking about not accepting this karmic being as the whole of the self experience.
Later another colleague told me it was probably a reference to a poem by Tolopa, a poem that Tolopa wrote for his student Naropa.
And of course, Trungpa Rinpoche loved Naropa and named his college institute after him, the Naropa Institute.
I thought you might enjoy hearing a little bit of this poem.
This is the song of Mahamudra.
Tolopa was, I forget, ninth or tenth century.
Yeah, tenth century.
What would it be to neither accept nor reject, to feel into our [unclear: "vow being"], without making that into another karmic thing?
So here's a little bit of Tolopa's poem.
*The illumination from an oil lamp lights the room instantly, even if it has been dark for eons.
Mind is boundless radiance.
How can the slightest darkness remain in a room of daily perception?
One who clings to mental processes cannot awaken to the radiance of mind,*
capital M, mind.
*Strenuously seeking truth by investigation and concentration, one will never appreciate the unthinkable simplicity and bliss that abides at the core.
To uncover this fertile ground, cut through the roots of complexity with the sharp gaze of naked awareness.
Remain entirely at peace, transparent and content.
You need not expend great effort, nor store up extensive spiritual power.
Remain in the flow of sheer awareness.*
*Mahamudra neither accepts nor rejects any current of energy, internal or external.*

Let's just hear that section again, because this is very much about our effort in sesshin, isn't it?
*The illumination from an oil lamp lights the room instantly, even if it has been dark for eons.

That was nice.
I actually noticed an absence of anger or shame.

That's the first part.

So I didn't have that experience.
But I did have the experience of becoming very absorbed in my mind, and just being caught.
I don't even remember what I was thinking exactly, but I withdrew from reality for a moment.
I had this moment of realizing I had blinked out.
I wasn't actually in the room.
And then Talus made this little gesture with his arms, a little gesture, and I felt myself flooding back into the room.
I realized I'd forgotten what the next thing I was supposed to do was: pass something.

I could not see it.
I did not know it was there.
I did not know where I was.

But then there are patterns of attention, and maybe those patterns become entrenched in some way.
So we're over and over not noticing, to where maybe our blind spot is, for all sakes and purposes, fairly substantial, fairly permanent, fairly solid.
We can't really see these blind spots, but we know from the evidence around us that they must exist.
Take the existence of cultural phenomena like sexism.
There couldn't be sexism if there weren't blind spots, right?
How could there be?
Maybe we're doing a little better.
We have reasonable gender diversity.
But also racism: our racial diversity is not so good if we look around.
And we don't know how we do that.
We don't.
I've been to meetings of white people sitting around trying to figure out why there are no non-white people.
I have.
And we can't figure it out.
We don't know.
But this phenomenon of not perceiving things is pretty impressive.
And there are some dramatic psychology experiments, which maybe you've heard of.
Now they're fairly well known, which maybe makes them sort of ignorable, because they're fairly well known.
But they're still very dramatic.
These are from the late nineties, early two-thousands.
So I guess high school and college introductory psychology classes probably mention these now.
They wouldn't have when most of us went to school, probably.
Two of them were conducted by the same research lab at Harvard.
Really creative people who got interested in this question of how we perceive.
What do we actually see?
You can see video excerpts of them online, I discovered recently.
Everything's online.
Here's one of them.
As a subject of the experiment, you're asked to sit down and watch a video.
You're told that on the video will be two teams passing a basketball back and forth.
One team has white shirts and one team has black shirts.
If you are very careful and really pay attention, you might be able to accurately count how many passes there are between the players with white shirts.
And we're analyzing how well you Harvard undergraduates can attend to this and count the passes between the players in white shirts.
Most of these studies, it turns out, are done with undergraduates because they're handy and cheap.

What the subjects are not told, and the video is maybe ten or fifteen minutes, I forget how long, is this: about halfway through the video, in the circle of college students passing basketballs in different shirts, with the basketballs moving, another college student dressed in a gorilla suit walks into the frame, turns towards the camera, and beats her chest.
It's a woman in the gorilla suit.
Then she walks off the frame.
Apparently they had to do several runs of that to get it so that the ball didn't hit the gorilla person.
And the other basketball players are ignoring the gorilla and just focusing on the game.
This has been replicated in various ways, in different groups, I guess.
Fifty percent of people do not see the gorilla.
Do not see the gorilla.
You ask them afterwards, "Anything unusual about the gorilla?"
"Oh no, fourteen passes.
Thanks, yeah, that was hard."
So what are the gorillas that we're not seeing?
It's not a matter of something being wrong with our eyes.
It's how we're attending, how we're paying attention.
So that's one.
And here's another.
If that's not evidence enough, this one's really funny.
I've talked about this one before because this one just cracks me up so much.
Also on Harvard.
And this is one of the ones where they pick on innocent people.
I don't know how the IRBs approve these things, like picking on innocent people.
Anyway, you're wandering around Harvard, some random person, and somebody walks up to you to ask directions.
They're, in fact, one of the experimenters, but you don't know that.
They just look like another Harvard person.
And you're somebody who knows Harvard, so you're picturing how to get to the such-and-so hall, and go around here and go around there.
And you're giving the directions.
And then there are some workers walking around, some kind of project going on.
And these two workers carrying a door interrupt your conversation and say "Excuse me, excuse me," and they walk in between the two of you.
Then they walk by, and you continue giving directions and finish up and go about your business.
In this case, about half the people fail to notice that there was a third person.
Two people are carrying this door.

You're talking to somebody, and it looks to you like two people carrying a door walk through.
There's actually a third person behind the door who switches with the person you're giving the directions to.
Totally different person.
I think the same gender.
I think they didn't push it that far, I don't remember.
I think the same gender, but different appearance, age, a different person.
And about half the people don't realize they're now talking to a different person.
I don't know how they thought of that.
Who would think that would work?
You wouldn't think that would work.
You think, oh, we just wasted a quarter and such and such research data, research money.
So these are different aspects of blind spots, maybe.
What's powerfully available to us as practitioners is that we can work with attention.
Attention is actually somewhat trainable, and maybe we can notice a little more of what's happening.
It might be like me with my rice spill.
We can become a little more aware when we are sucked into our karmic mind, our karmic life, and not actually available to the other beings on the planet who need our help.

We have access to the teachings of early Buddhism, which seem to be more or less oriented around how to deal with this troublesome karmic self.
What would be smart technologies of the mind to reduce suffering, increase awakening?

They don't.

The Buddha provided many lists of practices to free us a little bit from our preoccupation with our karmic self.

I'm not going to put that on the thing, but we'll just talk about five.
What I recently realized about these seven, which makes them easy to remember and maybe a little more useful, is that three of them are really oriented around effort.

The work of practice.
These three we've been very engaged with, no matter what.
If you've been sitting here, you've been engaged with them.

Investigate, notice what's happening.

If our karmic stance is characterized by lack, and it sadly so often is, it sounds like things we're missing, things we need to work on.
I remember one time in a sesshin, pretty far into a longer sesshin, I think it must have been, Norman made a big point about work, the work of practice.
He said something like, "Consider what it is you're working on."
Now cut it out.
Don't work.
So on one side of these seven factors, maybe we think of it like a balance beam.
On the one side is this joyful effort of investigating, being diligent, being curious, bringing forward our energy, entering into this situation wholeheartedly, right?
Wholeheartedly, we say, on one side.
And maybe the pivot of the little balance beam for these seven factors that support awakening is the factor of mindfulness.
Remembering that we're practicing, noticing what's happening, bringing ourselves back, bringing ourselves back.
So our balance beam, if we're working hard in practice, is jumping off of this peg, off of this pivot point, with investigation, diligence, joy, ho, ho, ho, and we're a little off balance, right?
We're a little worked up.
We're really pretty darn tired at the end of sesshin.
How are you?
Right?
So maybe our effort's been a little off balance.
We're that tired, that exhausted.
Another way you look at it is: what did you do all day that you're so tired?
Nothing.
On the other side of the balance beam, we have three factors that are more grounding, calming, gathering, discerning.

These three are calm itself, concentration, or samadhi, and wisdom. [unclear: "shohaku"], and speaking a lot about wisdom through Norman's talks, I thought we might look a little bit at calm and see if we can practice calm this afternoon.
Master Sheng Yan translates this factor as lightness and ease.
Lightness and ease.
So here's where our karmic self has to just imagine into our vow self a little bit, imagine the possibility.
Right now, do it.
The possibility that there's lightness and ease in the body, in the mind, in the heart.
One way to look at these factors is as something that's already there.
It's really there.
And maybe it's a little occluded, maybe we need to remind ourselves to notice the presence of this factor.

The other thing that working with these factors helps us with is this: we notice it's very frustrating to try to work with them if we're too caught in our usual dualistic way of thinking about our karmic self.
Usually we think something's all this way or all that way, right?
"I'm tired, I'm upset" is one way.
"Calm and happy" is another way, and never the twain shall meet, right?
Unless the conditions were radically different and they would just fix it on schedule and give us yoga and proper support and so on and so on.
But it might be that as we work with these factors we can investigate the possibility that they're a little more intermingled than that.
Maybe right in the middle of tired, aching, grouchy, there's also lightness and ease there.
Could be.
I don't want to say "could be", I hope so.
So find out for yourself.
Another way to work with this factor of calm or lightness and ease is with the wonderful practice of permission.
The wonderful practice of permission: giving ourselves permission to be just how we are.

Thank you to him.

What happens with your mental factors when I suddenly shift it like that?

Zen is an adjective, Zen.
